records.title: LOCKDOWN
records.abstract: A household survival game set during a pandemic lockdown. Each day you open the delivery, read messages from family and the news, keep the fridge in order, and cook for everyone at home. Cooking is a spatial puzzle: cut ingredients into shapes and fit them into the pan, tangram style.
findings: Cooking as a tangram-like puzzle: cut, rotate and fit ingredient pieces into the pan.
Fridge storage as a grid inventory where food spoils if left too long.
Daily loop of deliveries, family messages and news that shape what the household needs.

gallery.caption: The apartment, day six
Meal preparation: fitting cut ingredients into the pan
Fridge storage
Daily news

study.pitch: LockDown is a household survival game set in one small apartment during a city lockdown with no announced end. Each day the player fits the delivered food into a pan as a spatial puzzle, stores what is left in a fridge that can rot, and answers the family and the building on the phone.

sections.heading: Where the rules come from
body: LockDown is about slowly losing control while you wait for something with no announced end. The idea comes from my family's 2022 lockdown in Shanghai. We ate whatever came in the supply package, my grandparents needed medicine that nobody was allowed to go and get, and nobody told us when it would end.

I use those memories as design rules. The player receives supplies instead of shopping. The apartment never grows. Food, medicine and the neighbors' requests all come out of one small reserve. The run lasts twenty days, but the screen shows the day number with no countdown.

The cooking puzzle starts from the traditional Chinese tangram. Here the shapes are ingredients and the space is a pan or a fridge, and the gaps and leftovers show the shortage without a line of dialogue.
sections.summary: LockDown comes from my family's 2022 Shanghai lockdown. I turned those memories into rules: supplies arrive instead of shopping, the flat never grows, and twenty days pass with no countdown.

media.caption: Day 12 in the same small apartment, with no countdown shown.

sections.heading: One day, one meal
body: Each morning starts with yesterday's consequences. Everyone loses 2 morale and 1 health, the fridge is checked for rot, and a package arrives. By Day 7 the bag can be just noodles, a cabbage and some rice.

The player reads the phone, plans the meal, fits the food into the pan and serves it. Leftovers go into the fridge if they fit and are lost if they don't. Before Day 3 there is no fridge, and only the largest leftover keeps on the counter. Sleep moves the day on but resets nothing.

media.caption: The daily loop from the GDD, where each pass starts from whatever the last day left behind.
The Day 7 package: noodles, a cabbage and rice for three people.
Day 1 morning, with the first package waiting to be picked up.
Day 6 after dinner: time to rest before the next day.

sections.summary: Each morning carries yesterday's consequences. The player reads the phone, fits food into the pan, serves, and stores the leftovers that fit. Sleep moves the day on but resets nothing.

sections.heading: A pan that is never big enough
body: I built the game around a pan rather than a resource screen, because every problem in the house ends up at dinner. A resource screen would turn Grandpa's tablets into a number. The pan turns them into a space that is too small.

The twelve ingredients are shapes of 3 to 7 cells, each with its own calories and nutrients. A cabbage is a five-cell cross worth 25 kcal, and pork takes seven cells and gives 250. A meal is scored against a 470 kcal target: 38% balance, 24% calories, 20% total nutrients and 18% pan filled. Under 42% nobody recovers health, and under 28% everyone gets weaker.

Until Day 6 there is no knife, so the pan is a plain rectangle and every piece goes in whole. After that the pan is an irregular shape of roughly 18 to 25 cells, always with a solid 3 by 3 core so the largest piece fits. The knife cuts along the grid, and the part you don't cook goes to the fridge.

media.caption: The meal screen, with ingredient shapes on the left, the pan in the middle, the fridge on the right and the 470 kcal target along the top.
Day 6, when the new knife splits a piece of tofu along the grid before it goes into the irregular pan.
Before the knife, whole pieces fill a plain rectangular pan.
Later, pork, tofu and egg share an irregular pan.

sections.summary: I built the game around a pan, because every problem in the house ends at dinner. From Day 6 a knife cuts along the grid and the pan turns irregular.

sections.heading: Storage that turns into a chore
body: Each new rule arrives through something in the house. On Day 1 the fridge is broken, and the next day Aunt Li complains in the building group about Grandpa dragging it around at midnight. On Day 3 he gets it working and storage unlocks. After two days of cooking everything at once, the player knows what a fridge is for.

The fridge is a 6 by 8 grid. On Day 7 the building loses power, and from Day 8 anything stored for two days grows a rotten cell. Each morning a rotten cell spreads to the next cell of the same item 62% of the time and into a touching item 35% of the time.

Rot never deletes food. The good cells can still be cooked, or cut away from the bad ones. The grade ignores rot on purpose. Every rotten cell in the pan costs each person 4 health, up to 14 a meal, so an S meal with rot in it still makes the family ill.

media.caption: The fridge on Day 8, where the dark olive cells are rot that has crossed between items where they touch.
Day 3: Grandpa says to put spare food in the fridge.
The repaired fridge on Day 3: 48 empty cells.

sections.summary: The fridge unlocks on Day 3. From Day 8 stored food rots and spreads. The grade ignores rot, so an S meal can still make the family ill.

sections.heading: Three at home, five in the building chat
body: In 2022 there were five of us at home. For the game I cut the household to three: Grandpa, whose health depends on things from outside, Daughter, who says out loud what everyone feels, and the player, with no name or face, who makes the decisions. Director Zhang, Mr. Wang, Aunt Li, Uncle Yu and the 6F Stranger reach the flat through the building chat.

Grandpa starts on 60 health and loses 5 more every morning until his medicine is secured. On Day 5 his last box is empty. Aunt Li checks her own drawer, and half the time her strip is empty too. The 6F Stranger can get the pills sooner for two things from the fridge, and the chat names the two the game took.

On Day 8 Daughter has a fever of 38.2. A warm meal from a fridge item gives her 25 health, and letting her rest costs her 20. On Day 13 Zhang asks for food for the sealed seventh floor. On Day 18 taking Daughter downstairs early works 60% of the time, and if the patrol stops them, everyone loses 12 morale.

media.caption: Day 5 in the building chat, where the 6F Stranger takes two fridge items for the medicine and the chat names which two.
Day 13, when 7F is sealed and each answer says what it will cost.
Day 8: Daughter has a fever, and the player chooses porridge.
Day 18: take Daughter downstairs early, or wait for the assigned time.

sections.summary: I cut my real household of five to three: Grandpa, Daughter and a faceless player. Five neighbors reach the flat through the building chat, and their requests cost food.

sections.heading: The phone and the screen
body: The phone has three channels at three distances: the city newspaper, the building group and the family chat. Often they cover the same problem. On Day 4 Zhang asks every flat for its medicine doses, on Day 5 the paper reports refills running late, and that morning Grandpa finds his box empty.

The HUD shows the day and each person's health. After dinner one family member answers in a single line, the weakest one when the meal went badly, and that is how the player learns what the family thinks of the food. A meal with rot in it gets "That tastes off. Is it still fresh?" The letter grade sits behind a small Last meal toggle. On Day 20 the lockdown simply ends, and the report shows the days at home and each person's health.

media.caption: The final report after Day 20, with the days at home and each person's health.
The Day 5 paper reports medicine refills running late.
After dinner, one family member answers in a single line.

sections.summary: The phone's three channels often report the same problem from different distances. The HUD shows the day and health, and the family's reaction comes as one line after dinner.

sections.heading: What I'd build next
body: In the next build the knife slowly goes blunt. Hard ingredients wear it down faster, a blunt knife only cuts soft food like tofu or cabbage, and sharpening it depends on a neighbor lending a stone. Cut surfaces spoil faster than whole ingredients. On outage days the spoilage clock advances twice and the fridge hum cuts out.

Choices should also reach further. In that build the player picks which two items go to the 6F Stranger, and he comes back on Day 13 expecting the same deal. If Daughter was left to rest, her fever returns on Day 14. 7F sends something back on Day 17 only if they were helped. If the patrol catches the family on Day 18, no package arrives on Day 19.
sections.summary: Next I want the knife to wear out and choices to come back later: the 6F Stranger returns, the fever recurs, and a failed Day 18 trip costs a package.

gallery.caption: The dining table where every meal ends up.
Day 7, the apartment before cooking at the counter.
Day 5: Grandpa finds his medicine box empty.

records.title: Trail Adventure
records.abstract: A first-person game about climbing and wildlife photography. An old photographer leaves you his cabin, his camera and a mountain island. Pack your bag, climb any rock face, creep up on the animals, and send your best shots to the people who live on the island.
findings: Climb anywhere steeper than 50°, on one stamina bar that hunger, cold, tiredness, injury and bag weight each eat into.
Photos are scored from one to three stars (close-ups, flight, eye contact, golden hour) and fill a field guide of 24 species.
The island, its cave and the old mine are generated in the editor, and the whole journal-style interface is drawn in code.

gallery.caption: Leo’s cabin, where every trip starts
Creeping up on deer by the pond
Dusk at a campfire
Photos and postcards brought home

study.pitch: Trail Adventure is a first-person game about climbing a mountain island with an old camera. The player packs a bag in the cabin, climbs any rock face on one stamina bar, and photographs 24 species for the people who live on the island.

sections.heading: A climb that costs something
body: The part I care about is the climb. I want it to cost something, so that a goat photographed on a high ledge is remembered together with the way up to it.

The idea comes from my own trips. On Mount Rainier a marmot watched me from a ridge in the fog, and I only saw it because I had walked a long way up to where it lived. My photos from that trip are the first pages of Leo's Journal, the book by the armchair in the cabin. I use those trips as design rules.
points: The animals live away from the path, so the player has to go up to them.
Going up is tiring, and tiredness is what ends a trip.
Animals leave when they see you, so a good photo takes waiting.
What I keep from a trip is what I brought back, so the game has a cabin that keeps it.

media.caption: The title screen, where she sits in the armchair over Leo's Journal with the mountain outside the window.
Leo's cabin, where every trip starts and ends.

sections.summary: I want the climb to cost something, so a photo is remembered with the way up. The rules come from my own mountain trips.

sections.heading: A trip
body: Every trip starts and ends in the cabin. She packs up to four tools at the bench, reads the weather card in the window, and picks a start on the wall map, at the trailhead or at a fire she has found. I put this at home on purpose. By the time she opens the door she has already made a few decisions about the day.

On the mountain she climbs, creeps up on animals and takes photos. People at the fires ask for photos, she sends them from the phone on her wrist, and what they give back comes down on a paper parachute. A night at a fire brings a fresh roll of film. The trip ends at the summit, when she picks Go home, or when she is too worn out to go on.
points: What to carry: four places in the bag, and every tool adds weight.
Move or wait: stamina comes back fast, but hunger and tiredness build all day.
Shoot or wait: a roll has ten shots, and a blurred photo scores half.

media.caption: One trip, with the screen she sees at each step, from packing at home to resting at a fire and coming back.
The wall map, where she picks the day's start.
A fire on the mountain, where a night brings fresh film.

sections.summary: Each trip starts and ends in the cabin, so the player makes the day's choices before opening the door.

sections.heading: The mountain is the obstacle
body: The first version had set obstacles on the trails and a die roll to get past each one, and the walking between them was dead time. I replaced all of that with climbing. Any face steeper than 50 degrees can be climbed by holding the left mouse button.

Walking is free. Running costs 2.5 stamina a second, climbing up to 4, hanging still 2, a jump 5, and a lunge up the face with Space 20 at once for 1.7 metres. A second after she stops spending, the bar comes back at 20 a second. I made walking free so that players look at the mountain while they walk, not at the bar.

Five afflictions each take a coloured slice off the end of the bar: hunger, tiredness, cold, injury and the weight of the bag. The bar shrinks a slice at a time, so the player can see what took each one, and most of them can be dealt with.
points: The Down Jacket cuts cold to 30 percent.
The Flashlight is the only light in the cave. If it pushes the Down Jacket out of the bag, the snow above the mine is a much harder climb.

media.caption: Mid-climb, with both hands on the rock and the stamina bar along the bottom.
Evening at the Snow Fire, where hunger and cold have each taken a marked slice off the end of the bar.

sections.summary: Climbing replaced set obstacles. Any face over 50° can be climbed, walking is free, and five afflictions each take a visible slice off the stamina bar.

sections.heading: Keeping still and waiting
body: The right mouse button brings the camera up and the left button takes the shot. The score comes from what is in the frame: getting close, a bird in flight, an animal looking at the lens, a mother with her young, golden hour. The points add up to one, two or three stars. Moving shakes the camera and a blurred photo scores half, so the good photos come from keeping still.

Each species in the field guide has a row of moments, from first sight and a close-up to the things only that animal does. A new moment earns a star, and stars are the only currency, so an animal she has already photographed is still worth finding again.

The 24 species do not all react the same way. A boar charges, a squirrel runs up a tree, foxes steal snacks, and the owl only comes out between 17:30 and 6:30. If every animal ran off the same way, players would learn one trick and use it on all of them.

media.caption: A three-star deer photo by the pond, with the moments the guide already has listed on the card.
The field guide open at the fox, with all eight of its moments on film.

sections.summary: The score comes from what is in the frame, and moving blurs the shot, so good photos come from keeping still. Each of the 24 species reacts differently.

sections.heading: Sixteen people and Leo's camera
body: The player is a young woman with no name. Leo, an old photographer who walked this mountain for forty years, has left her his camera and a letter, and she lives in his cabin. "It's yours now," he writes. Sixteen people on the island make 38 requests between them. The eight tools come out of six of those stories, so every new ability has a person behind it.

Nell waits at the cave mouth and will not go past the daylight. She tells the player that Shepherd Bram has a flashlight. Without one, the player feels her way along the wall inside at a little over half speed. Bram's last request is the ducks on the pond, and that photo brings the Flashlight down by parachute. With a light the cave opens up: nine species, and Old Ida deep in the old mine.
Old Marten knew Leo. His last request is a ptarmigan close enough to count its feathers. When the photo works, his postcard is waiting at home: "We never did get that ptarmigan. You did."

media.caption: Nell at the cave mouth, telling the player where to find a flashlight.
Old Ida in the Miners' Camp, deep in the old mine.
Shepherd Bram asks for a photo of a duck.
A reward coming down on a paper parachute.

sections.summary: Sixteen islanders make 38 requests, and the eight tools come from six of their stories, so every new ability has a person behind it.

sections.heading: What the cabin keeps
body: After a real trip I come home with photos and a few things to remember it by, so the cabin keeps them. A finished story sends a postcard, with her photo on the front and a note and a crayon drawing on the back. A carving of a species can be ordered for the Carver's Shelf once every moment of it is in the guide, and stars buy parts for Leo's camera at the bench.

The interface follows the same idea. The HUD, the panels and the field guide look like a travel journal, with paper, washi tape, rubber stamps and sticker icons where text labels would normally go. The wrist phone is a device, so it keeps a clean screen.

media.caption: The back of Rowan's postcard, with a note and a crayon hedgehog.
The wrist phone sending a goat photo to Kofi on its clean screen.
The Carver's Shelf, one carving for each completed species.
Fitting new parts to Leo's camera at the bench.

sections.summary: The cabin keeps what each trip brings back: postcards, carvings and camera parts. The interface looks like a travel journal, except the wrist phone.

sections.heading: What I'd build next
body: At the moment only the owl keeps set hours. The next build makes the time of day part of planning a trip.
points: The hedgehog comes out towards dusk and deer are easiest to find early in the morning, so requests that mention a time depend on it.
An owl that roosts during the day, so players who never stay out after dark can still find one asleep in a tree.
Ambient occlusion for the faceted rock and the cave, and depth of field in the viewfinder.
sections.summary: Next, I want the time of day to matter when planning a trip, not only for the owl.

gallery.caption: The cabin with its bed, coats and island map.
Photos and postcards pinned up on the cabin wall.

download.label: Windows build, 1 Nov 2026 (Google Drive). Unzip and run Trail Adventure.exe.

records.title: Last Mile
records.abstract: A ten-day management game about running a neighbourhood delivery station. Each wave of orders lands on a live 3D city as countdown pins, and you decide who takes them: riders, robots or drones. Speed is only half the job; heavy loads, stairs, fatigue and the riders' own lives all weigh on every assignment.
findings: Real-time dispatch on a 3D city: routing modes, traffic, rush hours, fatigue and heavy loads all change who should take an order.
A small cast of riders with their own stories, written in a dry corporate voice, and choices that carry from one day to the next.
A procedurally laid-out city with a day-night cycle and automated play-through checks in the editor; the illustrations and landmark models are AI-generated and assembled by editor scripts.

gallery.caption: Title screen: the station at dawn
Morning rush: orders as countdown pins over the city
Assigning an order: time left, ETA and who can take it
Day one briefing

study.pitch: Last Mile is a ten-day management game about running Lanting, a small food-delivery station. Orders land on a 3D city as countdown pins, and for each one the player decides who takes it: a rider who is paid by the drop, a ground robot or a drone.

sections.heading: Each order is someone's pay
body: The riders are paid by the drop, so sending Chen instead of Xiaoyu on an ID check decides which of them gets closer to the bill they are saving for. Over the ten days headquarters moves the station onto robots and drones.

The first version was a policy game with sliders for pay and late fees, and a pay cut was spread over everyone, so nobody in particular lost anything. I changed it so the player hands out every order by hand to riders with names.
points: The board counts parcels, so a crate counts the same as a coffee.
Each machine fixes one problem and leaves another.
AO-6, the assistant from day 6, never overrules the player.
sections.summary: Riders are paid by the drop, so I have the player hand out every order by hand. Over ten days headquarters moves the station onto machines.

media.caption: The title screen: the desk in the depot, with Zhou Heng's first text on the phone.

sections.heading: A day at the station
body: The station gets ¥180 each morning. The player can save it, or spend ¥80 to coach the rider who knows the streets least, ¥90 on breakfast and a rest, or ¥50 to add 15 seconds to the first four orders.

A shift is two 90-second waves. On day 1 six orders arrive one at a time. From day 2 each wave opens with two orders and the rest land in a burst from 36 seconds in, while the first riders are still out, so someone has to wait. Orders rise to 16 a day by day 7. Between waves the player can pay ¥40 for 20 more seconds on new orders, or take ¥60 of rush money that cuts 15 seconds and adds one to the target.

Each rider costs ¥30 in wages at night. The report puts delivered against target next to what each rider took home, so a good day for the station and a bad day for one rider sit on the same page. A station that can't pay wages closes, and the player replays that morning.

media.caption: One day: orders, calls and dispatches repeat through both waves, the report closes the shift, and the next morning starts on the phone.
The morning on day 4: the day's facts, the team and the morning plans on the phone.
The report on day 4: 12 delivered against a target of 10, and what each rider was paid.

sections.summary: Each day the station gets ¥180 and runs two 90-second waves of orders. At night each rider costs ¥30, and a station that can't pay closes.

sections.heading: Choosing who takes the order
body: Clicking a pin lists who could take the order, with an arrival estimate. A card for someone who can't go is locked and says why, and the clock holds until the player chooses.

The deadline comes from the fastest rested courier on the ground who could take the order, times about 1.4 on day 2 and 1.2 by day 10. I based it on the best courier so that a slower pick, or an order left waiting, is what makes it late. Orders cancel 25 seconds after the deadline.

Each drop costs a rider 8 stamina on top of the ride, and a tired rider slows to 70% speed. Rest gives 12 seconds off and about 36 stamina. Waiting at the station gives nothing, so a break is something the manager has to give.
points: Standard: anyone. ¥6 to the station, ¥4 to the rider.
ID check: a rider, or from day 8 a robot with an ¥80 scanner. ¥8 and ¥5.
Sixth floor, no lift: a rider or a drone. ¥8 and ¥5.
Heavy restock: Strength 8. ¥10 and ¥6. A late drop halves both.

media.caption: Day 4: a breakfast for an old building without a lift. The drone is fastest, and the robot is locked because it can't climb stairs.

sections.summary: The player picks a courier for each order. The deadline is set by the fastest rested courier, so a slower pick or a wait makes it late.

sections.heading: Robots, drones and an assistant that learns
body: The robot arrives on day 3. It is never paid per drop, but it can't climb stairs or check an ID. That night headquarters compares it with the riders on standard orders. If the riders were on time more often, the player can send it back. A tie goes to the robot.

The drone comes on day 4. It flies straight over the blocks and is the fastest courier on the map, but it carries a load of 5 at most. If the robot stayed, headquarters wants 2 machines on the roster from day 6, 3 from day 8 and 4 on day 10, out of six places, so every machine takes a rider's place.

From day 6 AO-6 recommends someone for every order. Each Confirm, or each time the player picks someone else, is saved as an example. It keeps the last 96 and cites them: "This follows what you did on Day 6, #1058." I wanted the player to train it willingly, one Confirm at a time.

media.caption: How AO-6 learns: each Confirm, or each time the player picks someone else, is saved as an example for that kind of order.

sections.summary: Robots arrive on day 3 and drones on day 4, each taking a rider's place. From day 6 AO-6 recommends someone for each order and learns from every choice.

sections.heading: Four riders and what they are saving for
body: Each rider has three scores out of 10: Streets for speed, Strength for load, Judgment for tricky handovers. Chen is 9, 4 and 9. Ajie is 5, 9 and 5. Lin is 8, 6 and 6. Xiaoyu joins on day 2 at 4, 6 and 8.

Each is short of money for one thing by one evening: Xiaoyu ¥30 for a room deposit by day 4, Lin ¥40 rent by day 5, Ajie ¥50 he owes a friend by day 6, Chen ¥80 for his wife's medicine by day 9. A fair share of the work just covers it. On the evening her deposit is due, Xiaoyu asks for an order and stops halfway: "Could I... sorry. Could I take this one?" If she falls short she loses the room and starts every shift 20 seconds late.

From day 2 one rider calls each evening about something the board doesn't count. Ajie asks for small parcels, because "the board counts parcels, not weight." I kept one rule for the writing: the riders talk about crates, rent and doorbells, and only AO-6 and headquarters carry the satire.

media.caption: Day 4: Xiaoyu asks for an order on the evening her deposit is due.
Lin asks to finish what he is carrying and skip the evening rush to pick up his daughter.

sections.summary: Each of the four riders needs money for one thing by a set evening, and a fair share of the work just covers it.

sections.heading: A district built from one road graph
body: The map is modelled on Xujiahui: 26 hand-placed junctions around a six-armed crossing, with eight outer districts generated as five-by-five street grids. Orders go to four of them, among them Willow Bend and Heron Road.

An editor script finds each closed block in the road graph, lines its edges with lots and fills the middle with a grid turned to the longest side. The ordinary buildings are built in code. The landmarks and vehicles are AI-generated models that editor scripts fit into the blocks.
The light follows the shift from warm morning to blue evening, but the interface keeps its colours, so a red countdown at dusk looks the same as one at breakfast.

media.caption: The rain alert on day 4, over the map.
Ajie on the walkie-talkie about a moved drop-off, out in the city.

sections.summary: The map is a road graph modelled on Xujiahui: 26 hand-placed junctions and eight generated districts, with blocks and ordinary buildings filled in by code.

sections.heading: Lessons on the map, and ten days played by the editor
body: Day 1 teaches by doing. Zhou Heng, the regional manager, walks the player through the first dispatch, and later lessons appear the first time they are needed, such as Strength on the first full crate.

The editor can also play the trial by itself. A scripted manager runs all ten days on the real roads and traffic, and the run fails if any of the 132 orders doesn't end in a delivery or a cancellation, if traffic stops, if two bodies overlap, or if a story call is left open.

media.caption: The ticket before the evening wave: keep it standard, buy extra time or take rush pay.

sections.summary: Day 1 teaches through a guided first dispatch, and the editor can play all ten days itself to check that all 132 orders end in a delivery or cancellation.

records.title: Sniff & Snitch
records.abstract: An online co-op stealth game for two. Lyra, a witch, and Fia, a red panda, are both in for theft, and the only way out of the magic prison is together: split up to take each one's own route, slip past guards who can see and hear you, and meet again at doors that need you both. Get caught and you are marched to a cage; your partner has until the gas fills it to break you out.
findings: Guard AI that sees and hears: noise from jailbreaks and thrown objects draws guards over, and the two players can mark a guard and take them down together.
Capture and rescue: a caught player is escorted to a gas cage and the partner has to hold to break them out in time, with its own HUD, escape UI and game-over flow.
Co-op systems over Netcode with the server deciding shared state: doors, lifts and boxes that need both players, a ping system, throwing, quests, save points and the character select.

study.pitch: An online co-op stealth game for two: Lyra, a witch, and Fia, a red panda, are both in for theft and have to break out of a magic prison together. I was a programmer and designer on the capstone team and built the guard AI, the capture and rescue loop, and many of the co-op systems.

facts.label: Engine
facts.value: Unity 6, C#, Netcode for GameObjects, Unity Relay

facts.label: Platform
facts.value: PC, online co-op for two players

sections.heading: Two thieves, one way out
body: Lyra and Fia are both in for theft, and neither of them gets out of the prison alone. Each player claims one of them on the character select screen, and the run starts once both roles are taken.

We built the two of them to be good at different things. Lyra is 1.8 m tall, drags boxes, and can put on a mask that keeps guards from growing suspicious of her. Fia is 1.0 m tall, jumps 1.4 m to Lyra's 1.0, climbs ledges and can dash 3.5 m. Some magic barriers stop only one of them, marked with a paw or a witch icon, so most rooms have a route for each.

media.caption: Character select: each player picks a mugshot card.
Fia's mugshot card on the character select screen.

sections.summary: Lyra and Fia escape a magic prison together. Each player takes one, and their different heights, jumps and skills give most rooms a separate route for each.

sections.heading: Split up, then meet at the door
body: The first stretch of Level 1 gives Lyra and Fia a "Find a way out" step each. The two run in parallel, and only when both are done does the next step appear: "Meet at the door".

Each character also has an exit of their own, and the level is won only when both players are standing in theirs. A checkpoint saves only after every connected player has walked into it, so a restart always brings the two of them back to the same checkpoint.

media.caption: The success screen, shown when both players reach their exits.

sections.summary: Lyra and Fia work in parallel, then regroup. The next quest step, winning the level and saving a checkpoint all wait for both players.

sections.heading: Guards that see and hear
body: I built the guard AI. Each guard is one state machine with 18 states and a suspicion meter from 0 to 1. He sees 12.3 m in a 120 degree cone. An unmasked player within 2.8 m fills the meter in one second, and at the edge of his sight in about 1.8 seconds.

Hearing is a separate system. Crouching carries 4 m, walking 10 m and running 16 m. The first 5 m of a sound pass through walls at full strength, and each wall after that halves what is left, so Fia running behind one wall is heard out to 10.5 m instead of 16.

A noise can pull a guard off his patrol, but it cannot interrupt a guard who is already watching someone. I set it up this way so a thrown coin has to be planned before a guard looks at you; once he is watching, it does nothing.
sections.summary: I built the guard AI: one state machine per guard that sees in a cone and hears through walls, with each wall halving what is left past 5 m.

sections.heading: Fifteen seconds in the gas cage
body: Getting caught does not end the run. The guard cuffs the player and walks them to his cage. During the escort their camera sits 35 degrees off the guard's right shoulder, because from straight behind, the guard hides the player walking in front of him.

In the cage, green gas thickens as time runs down. The partner has 15 seconds to get there and hold E for 1.5 seconds. Opening the lock makes a 14 m noise, and for 20 seconds any guard who sees the empty cage comes to check. When Fia frees Lyra with the gas nearly full, the clang of the lock turns the nearest guard toward them as they run.

If the time runs out, or a guard catches the second player while the first is still held, the level ends for both. I built the cage HUD for the free player: a cage icon tracks the partner across the screen and flashes faster as time runs out.

media.caption: The game over screen when the partner is not rescued in time.
Fia's game over card: "You have been captured."

sections.summary: Getting caught puts a player in a gas cage instead of ending the run. The partner has 15 seconds to free them, and the lock is loud.

sections.heading: Doors and boxes that need both of you
body: The latch door has one lever locked to Lyra and one to Fia, and opens only while both are down. The push box has a handle for each at their own height. Once both have grabbed, either player's W fills one shared ring, and ten taps slide the box 2.5 m. Pushed off a ledge, it becomes a step, and the landing reaches guards 25 m away. The lift door is a heavy gate they raise together, walk under, and let slam shut behind them for good.

The takedown needs both players too. A masked Lyra presses a seal onto an unaware guard, which weakens him for 6 seconds. In that window Fia drops onto him from at least 1.4 m above, and he is out for 12 seconds unless another guard walks up and wakes him.

For these mechanisms the server writes only who is gripping, how many taps have landed and when a sequence starts. Each machine works out the door height and the players' animations from that start time, so a player who joins late sees the same door and no animation has to be sent.
sections.summary: Latch doors, push boxes, the lift door and the takedown all need both players. The server syncs only grips, taps and start times; each machine animates the rest.

sections.heading: Pointing, throwing and keeping track
body: Middle mouse drops a ping on whatever is under the crosshair. Each player has one ping at a time, and it lasts 8 seconds. A ping on a guard sticks to him and moves with him, so the partner knows which guard is meant after he turns a corner.

Holding E lifts a crate overhead. A tap of the left mouse button tosses it 4 m, and holding for half a second throws it 8 m. The crate sits a set height above each character's own head, because a height measured on Lyra left Fia's crate floating a metre above her.

A teammate set up the first quest data and HUD. I turned each level's quests into node graphs of reach, interact and acquire steps, each assigned to Lyra, Fia, either or both, with the server deciding who completed each step. Character select is server-owned as well, and a player who drops out mid-level rejoins in whichever role is free.
sections.summary: Middle mouse pings a spot or a guard for 8 seconds, E lifts a crate to throw 4 or 8 m, and I turned quests into server-checked node graphs.

sections.heading: What I'd build next
body: Coins still use an older flat noise radius that ignores walls, and I want them on the same hearing model as footsteps. Lyra and Fia have separate entries in the noise table with the same values, and quieter steps for Fia would give the players a reason to send her ahead.

Every guard has a hearing multiplier, set to 1 in the current levels; I want to use it for a guard dog at 2.5. I also built a slow curse for guards who cannot reach a player, which slows the player to 45% speed for 3.5 seconds, and I want to place it where a player can stand out of reach.
sections.summary: Next, I want coins on the wall-aware hearing model, quieter steps for Fia, a guard dog with 2.5x hearing, and the slow curse placed in a level.
